name: Entrepreneurship
notes: Official knowledge areas verified 2026-10-11 from the 2026-2027 FBLA Entrepreneurship guideline (state copy of the national guideline, https://www.pafbla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/26-27-Entrepreneurship-PA.pdf): high school role play event (team of 1-3) with a 50-minute, 100-item objective test plus an interactive role play. Test areas and item counts: Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship (10), Discovery Strategies (15), Business Venture Concepts (20), Business Venture Resources (20), New Business Venture Activities (25), Business Law and Regulations (10), aligned to MBA Research EN/BL standards. The subs below are the earlier curriculum-based areas (business plan, marketing, finance and initial capital, legal and structure, operations and personnel, ethics/taxes/regulation) and have not yet been remapped to the official six. All questions are original practice items, U.S. conventions.

questions.q: A bakery owner wants to know whether customers will pay a premium for gluten-free bread before buying equipment. What is the best first step?
choices: Run a small pre-order or pilot test to measure demand
Buy a commercial oven and sign a 10-year storefront lease
Hire two full-time bakers before knowing demand
Sign a distribution contract with a national grocery chain
questions.explain: Validating demand cheaply before major spending reduces the risk of the business plan. Buying equipment, hiring or signing big contracts first commits money before demand is known.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, which category describes an internal advantage the business has over its competitors?
questions.explain: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. Strength is the internal advantage.

questions.q: A company gives its basic app away for free and charges only for premium features. Which business model is this?
questions.explain: Freemium pairs a free base offering with paid upgrades. Subscription-only would charge for all access from the start.

questions.q: Which is the best description of a target market?
choices: All consumers who might ever buy any product
Only the people who live closest to the business
A specific group of customers with shared needs that the business chooses to serve
questions.explain: A target market is a chosen, defined group. Trying to serve everyone is a common planning mistake.

questions.q: Which type of feasibility study asks whether the owner has the equipment, skills and suppliers needed to deliver the product?
questions.explain: Operational feasibility tests capability to produce and deliver. Market feasibility tests demand; financial feasibility tests funding and returns.

questions.q: A product sells for $25 per unit, has a variable cost of $15 per unit and fixed costs of $12,000 per year. How many units must be sold to break even?
questions.explain: Contribution per unit is $25 minus $15, or $10, so $12,000 divided by $10 is 1,200 units. Dividing by the $25 price gives the wrong answer of 480.

questions.q: Why is the executive summary of a business plan usually written last, even though it appears first?
choices: It is a legal requirement that must be signed last
It replaces the financial projections for lenders
It summarizes the key findings and the funding request from every other section
It lists every employee and job title in order of seniority
questions.explain: The summary can only be accurate once the rest of the plan is complete. It does not replace any section.

questions.q: A new coffee shop opens near two national chains that charge less. Which strategy best supports a sustainable position?
choices: Match the chains' prices to win price-sensitive customers
Offer the widest possible menu to appeal to everyone
Copy the chains' menu and open a location next to each one
Focus on an unmet need, such as locally roasted specialty drinks, and charge for the difference
questions.explain: Differentiation on a need the chains do not serve is more defensible than a price war the shop cannot win.

questions.q: Which best describes a value proposition?
choices: The specific benefit a customer receives that makes the offer worth choosing
The total value of the company's assets on its balance sheet
The price printed on the product label
The company's mission statement written for employees
questions.explain: A value proposition states why a customer should choose this offer over alternatives, which is about benefit rather than price or assets.

questions.q: A founder builds a simple landing page to test sign-ups before building the full product. This approach is best described as:
questions.explain: A minimum viable product is the simplest version that tests whether customers want the idea, before full investment.

questions.q: Which term describes the portion of the total market a new business can realistically capture in its first few years?
choices: The gross domestic product share of the industry
questions.explain: TAM is the whole market, SAM is the part the business can serve, and SOM is the realistic share it can win. The word realistically points to SOM.

questions.q: The threat that customers can easily switch to a substitute product is part of which analysis framework?
questions.explain: Porter's model includes the threat of substitutes among five competitive forces; the others are not competitive-analysis frameworks.

questions.q: In the BCG growth-share matrix, a product with high market share in a low-growth market is classified as a:
questions.explain: Cash cows generate more cash than they need in a mature market. Stars have high share and high growth.

questions.q: A bakery plans a second location two kilometres from its first. Much of the new location's projected sales would come from customers who would otherwise buy at the first. This risk is called:
questions.explain: Cannibalization is when a new outlet takes sales from an existing one, so total gain is smaller than the new location's sales suggest.

questions.q: A startup holds a patent but has few customers and needs capital. Which part of the business plan most directly shows investors how the patent will make money?
questions.explain: Investors need to see how the technology becomes income, which is what the revenue model and go-to-market plan show. Management, facilities and HR policies matter but do not answer that question.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a mission statement?
choices: We sell sandwiches, salads and soup at lunch
Our competitors are located on Main Street
To make healthy lunches affordable for every student at our school
questions.explain: A mission states purpose and who benefits. Describing products, financials or competitors does not state the purpose.

questions.q: Which factor most makes a competitive advantage sustainable over time?
choices: It is difficult for competitors to copy, such as a strong brand or a proprietary process
It relies on a low price that competitors can easily match
It depends on a single supplier who could leave
It is based on a temporary trend that fades quickly
questions.explain: Advantages last when rivals cannot easily imitate them. Easily matched prices or fragile supplier ties do not protect the business.

questions.q: Which element of the marketing mix refers to where the product is sold?
questions.explain: Place covers distribution channels and locations. Price, promotion and product are the other three of the 4 Ps.

questions.q: Which is an example of sales promotion?
choices: Changing the size of the package
Lowering the wholesale cost paid to suppliers
A coupon mailed to nearby households
Opening a warehouse in another state
questions.explain: Coupons are a sales promotion tool. Packaging, cost and distribution decisions belong to other mix elements.

questions.q: A 10 percent price increase causes quantity demanded to fall by 20 percent. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explain: Elasticity is the percent change in quantity divided by the percent change in price, 20 divided by 10, which is 2.0. Demand is elastic because the magnitude exceeds 1.

questions.q: Dividing a market by customers' lifestyles, values and interests is which type of segmentation?
questions.explain: Psychographic segmentation uses attitudes and lifestyle. Demographic uses measurable traits such as age and income.

questions.q: A company launches a new smartphone at a high price and lowers it over time as competitors enter. This strategy is called:
questions.explain: Skimming starts high to capture early adopters and drops later. Penetration starts low to gain share fast.

questions.q: A small firm has a $2,000 marketing budget and wants the lowest-cost awareness among local customers. Which choice fits best?
choices: A full-page print ad in a national magazine
A television commercial during prime time
Local social media ads and a Google Business Profile that collects reviews
Billboards on a highway 300 kilometres away
questions.explain: Local targeting and free profile listings give the most awareness per dollar for a small local budget.

questions.q: A customer spends $60 per month and stays for 5 years at a 40 percent gross margin. What is the approximate lifetime gross-margin value of this customer?
questions.explain: Annual spend is $720, five years is $3,600 of revenue, and 40 percent of that is $1,440. The $3,600 figure ignores margin.

questions.q: A brand name, logo or design that identifies a product and distinguishes it from others is called a:
questions.explain: Trademarks protect brand identifiers. Patents protect inventions, copyrights protect creative works, and a franchise is a business model.

questions.q: A business asks 300 customers to rate a new flavour on a 1-to-5 scale. This is which type of research?
questions.explain: Primary means new data collected directly, and quantitative means numerical ratings. Focus groups would be qualitative.

questions.q: In which stage of the product life cycle do sales grow fastest and competitors enter?
questions.explain: Growth is marked by rapid sales increases and new entrants. Introduction has slow sales and maturity has flattening sales.

questions.q: Which is an example of publicity rather than paid advertising?
choices: A paid radio spot during the morning drive
A printed flyer distributed for a fee
A local newspaper writing a story about the grand opening
questions.explain: Publicity is unpaid media coverage the business does not control. Any paid placement is advertising.

questions.q: A manufacturer sells directly to consumers through its own website. Which distribution channel is this?
questions.explain: A direct channel skips intermediaries. The others all include at least one middleman.

questions.q: A customer buys a product mainly because a friend recommended it. This is most influenced by:
questions.explain: Peer recommendation is social influence. Price, packaging and loyalty programs are other drivers.

questions.q: Which is the main risk of relying on frequent discounts?
choices: It always raises the cost of goods sold
It trains customers to wait for sales and erodes brand value
It is illegal under federal consumer law
questions.explain: Frequent discounting changes buying patterns and weakens perceived quality, though it does not directly change fixed costs.

questions.q: A perceptual map shows a brand positioned as premium and eco-friendly. This is best described as:
questions.explain: Positioning is how a brand is perceived relative to competitors. Segmentation divides the market; the others are different mix decisions.

questions.q: A retailer buys a jacket for $40 and sells it for $60. What is the markup as a percentage of cost?
questions.explain: Markup on cost is the $20 markup divided by the $40 cost, which is 50 percent. Dividing by the $60 selling price gives 33.3 percent, which is the markup on retail (gross margin), a common trap.

questions.q: A manufacturer gives retailers display allowances and extra margin so they will stock and recommend its new product. Which promotional strategy is this?
questions.explain: A push strategy aims promotion at channel members so they push the product toward consumers. A pull strategy aims promotion at consumers so they ask retailers for it.

questions.q: Which is an equity source of financing?
choices: Taking out a bank term loan
Using a bank line of credit
Selling an ownership stake to an angel investor
questions.explain: Equity means giving up ownership. Loans and trade credit are debt financing.

questions.q: Which equation is the basis of the balance sheet?
questions.explain: The accounting equation states that assets equal liabilities plus equity, and the balance sheet must balance on this basis.

questions.q: A business has revenue of $180,000, cost of goods sold of $70,000, operating expenses of $55,000 and income taxes of $10,000. What is net income?
questions.explain: Gross profit is $110,000, less $55,000 operating expenses gives $55,000, less $10,000 taxes gives $45,000. Stopping before taxes gives $55,000.

questions.q: Under accrual accounting, when is a sale recorded?
choices: Only when the customer pays in cash
When it is earned, regardless of when cash is received
Only when the year ends regardless of activity
At the moment the purchase order is issued
questions.explain: Accrual accounting recognizes revenue when earned, under the matching and revenue-recognition principles, not when cash moves.

questions.q: Current assets are $90,000 and current liabilities are $60,000. What is the current ratio?
questions.explain: The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities, $90,000 divided by $60,000, which is 1.5. Inverting the ratio gives 0.67.

questions.q: A business has fixed costs of $40,000 and a contribution margin ratio of 40 percent. What are the break-even sales in dollars?
questions.explain: Break-even sales equal fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio, $40,000 divided by 0.40, which is $100,000.

questions.q: A business has $50,000 in current assets and $38,000 in current liabilities. What is its working capital?
questions.explain: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, $50,000 less $38,000.

questions.q: A $50,000 truck has a $5,000 salvage value and a 5-year life. What is annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.explain: Straight-line depreciation is cost minus salvage value over useful life, $45,000 divided by 5, which is $9,000. Ignoring salvage gives $10,000.

questions.q: Which category on the statement of cash flows includes cash paid to buy new equipment?
questions.explain: Purchases of long-term assets are investing activities. Operating covers day-to-day income and expenses, and financing covers debt and equity.

questions.q: A bank loan requires a personal guarantee from the owner. What is the main added risk?
choices: The business's tax rate increases automatically
The owner must give up voting control
The owner's personal assets could be at risk if the business defaults
questions.explain: A personal guarantee makes the owner personally liable for the debt, which is a personal exposure rather than a tax or control change.

questions.q: Which statement shows a business's financial position at a specific point in time?
questions.explain: The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date. The income statement and cash flow statement cover a period.

questions.q: Revenue is $250,000 and cost of goods sold is $150,000. What is the gross profit margin?
questions.explain: Gross profit is $100,000, and $100,000 divided by $250,000 is 40 percent. The 60 percent figure is the cost ratio.

questions.q: A supplier offers terms of 2/10, net 30. A $1,000 invoice is paid on day 10. How much is paid?
questions.explain: Paying within the 10-day window takes a 2 percent discount, so $1,000 less $20 is $980.

questions.q: During a period of rising costs, which inventory method usually reports the highest net income?
questions.explain: FIFO assigns the older, cheaper costs to cost of goods sold when prices rise, so income is higher. LIFO does the opposite and is the trap; weighted average falls in between.

questions.q: A budget that compares planned figures with actual results is used to identify:
questions.explain: The gap between planned and actual amounts is the variance, which managers investigate.

questions.q: A $20,000 investment returns $5,000 of net profit in one year. What is the return on investment?
questions.explain: ROI is net profit divided by the investment, $5,000 divided by $20,000, which is 25 percent.

questions.q: A $100,000 loan carries 6 percent simple annual interest for 3 years. What is the total interest?
questions.explain: Annual interest is $6,000, and over 3 years on simple interest that is $18,000. The $6,000 figure is only one year.

questions.q: What is the main legal drawback of a sole proprietorship?
choices: The business must file a corporate tax return
The business must have at least three owners
The owner has unlimited personal liability for business debts
questions.explain: A sole proprietor and the business are legally one person, so personal assets are exposed. Hiring and tax filing are allowed.

questions.q: Which business structure gives owners limited liability and pass-through taxation by default?
questions.explain: An LLC shields owners from most business debts and, by default, its profits flow to owners' returns. A C corporation taxes entity profits separately.

questions.q: How is income of a C corporation taxed?
choices: Taxed only once at the shareholder level
Taxed at the entity level, and dividends are taxed again to shareholders
Not taxed if all profits are reinvested
Taxed only on capital gains realized by the owners
questions.explain: This is double taxation: corporate income tax, then tax on dividends. Pass-through entities avoid the first layer.

questions.q: A startup's website has original product photos and written product descriptions. Which intellectual property protects these automatically once they are created in a fixed form?
questions.explain: Copyright protects original creative works such as photos and text as soon as they are fixed in a tangible form; registration is optional. Patents cover inventions and trademarks cover brand identifiers.

questions.q: Under U.S. law, how long does a standard utility patent generally last?
questions.explain: U.S. utility patents run 20 years from filing. Copyright is the one tied to the author's life.

questions.q: Which is NOT generally required for a valid contract?
questions.explain: A contract needs offer, acceptance and consideration, plus capacity and lawful purpose. Notarization is not required for most contracts.

questions.q: Under the U.S. Uniform Commercial Code, a contract for the sale of goods priced at or above which amount generally must be in writing?
questions.explain: UCC section 2-201, the statute of frauds for goods, applies at $500 or more.

questions.q: Which federal law sets minimum wage and overtime rules in the United States?
questions.explain: The FLSA governs minimum wage, overtime and child labour. The others cover antitrust and securities.

questions.q: An agent signs a supply contract for a business owner, but the supplier has no idea the agent is acting for anyone else. Which agency-law concept describes this arrangement?
questions.explain: When the third party does not know a principal exists, the principal is undisclosed; the principal is still bound and can enforce the contract, and the agent can be held liable too. Apparent authority is a different agency concept about what a third party reasonably believes.

questions.q: A customer is injured by a defective product sold by a retailer. Under strict product liability, who can be held liable?
choices: The manufacturer and the retailer in the chain of distribution
Only the customer who used the product
The insurance company that wrote the policy
questions.explain: Strict product liability reaches every seller in the distribution chain for a defective product, regardless of fault.

questions.q: In a general partnership, what is each partner's liability for partnership debts?
choices: Joint and several, so each partner may be personally liable for all of it
Zero, because the partnership is separate
Only for debts they personally signed
questions.explain: General partners have unlimited joint and several liability. Limited liability is the feature of LLCs and some other structures.

questions.q: Which form of intellectual property protects confidential formulas such as a secret recipe, without registration?
questions.explain: Trade secrets are protected by keeping the information confidential. Registration would destroy that secrecy.

questions.q: A sole proprietor operates under a business name other than the owner's legal name. What must the owner typically do?
choices: Obtain a federal patent for the name
Register a copyright with the Library of Congress
Incorporate immediately to avoid the filing
File a doing-business-as (DBA) or assumed name certificate
questions.explain: A DBA or assumed name filing discloses the owner behind a trade name. A patent or copyright does not cover business names.

questions.q: A startup signs a commercial lease that requires it to pay base rent plus the property's taxes, insurance and maintenance. Which type of lease is this?
questions.explain: In a triple net lease the tenant pays base rent plus the three 'nets': property taxes, insurance and maintenance. In a gross lease the landlord covers those costs out of a single rent payment; a percentage lease adds a share of sales.

questions.q: Which federal law requires companies offering securities to the public to register them and disclose material information?
questions.explain: The 1933 Act governs public offerings and disclosure. The others cover antitrust and credit reporting.

questions.q: Which doctrine protects directors who make good-faith business decisions that later prove wrong?
questions.explain: The business judgment rule presumes good-faith, informed decisions are not second-guessed for poor outcomes.

questions.q: Which inventory system places a new order when stock falls to a preset level?
questions.explain: A reorder point is a set quantity that triggers an order. ABC analysis ranks items by value and does not trigger orders.

questions.q: What is the first step in recruiting new employees?
choices: Analyze the job and write a job description
Make a job offer to a candidate
questions.explain: A clear job analysis and description define what to recruit for. Offers, checks and interviews come later.

questions.q: Which formula calculates the economic order quantity (EOQ), where D is annual demand, S is ordering cost and H is holding cost per unit?
choices: The square root of (2DS divided by H)
questions.explain: EOQ balances ordering and holding costs and equals the square root of 2DS/H.

questions.q: In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need is at the bottom?
questions.explain: The hierarchy starts with basic physiological needs and moves up to self-actualization at the top.

questions.q: A manager makes decisions alone with minimal employee input. Which leadership style is this?
questions.explain: Autocratic leaders decide alone. Laissez-faire gives employees broad freedom and democratic leaders seek input.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a Gantt chart?
choices: To visualize a project timeline and the dependencies between tasks
To track customer demographics over time
questions.explain: A Gantt chart shows task durations, sequence and overlap over time. Break-even and satisfaction are different tools.

questions.q: A bakery's oven runs at full capacity during peak hours and customers wait. What is the best short-term operations response?
choices: Permanently double the number of ovens immediately
Shift some production to off-peak hours and take pre-orders for peak items
Reduce product quality to speed up production
Raise prices by 50 percent during peak hours
questions.explain: Shifting load and pre-ordering smooths demand at low cost. Doubling capacity is a long-term capital decision.

questions.q: Which quality tool uses a fishbone-shaped diagram to organize possible causes of a defect?
questions.explain: The Ishikawa diagram organizes causes by category around an effect. Pareto charts rank problems by frequency.

questions.q: What term describes the number of employees a manager directly supervises?
questions.explain: Span of control is the count of direct reports, which shapes how many layers an organization needs.

questions.q: A business averages 12 employees during the year, and 3 employees leave. What is the annual turnover rate?
questions.explain: Turnover rate is separations divided by average headcount, 3 divided by 12, which is 25 percent.

questions.q: Which training method has a new employee learn the job while working under a skilled coworker?
questions.explain: On-the-job training with a mentor builds skills in the real work setting. The others happen away from the job.

questions.q: A worker sets their own hours, uses their own tools and is paid per project. How is this worker most likely classified?
questions.explain: Control over how and when work is done and ownership of tools point to an independent contractor, which has tax and legal consequences.

questions.q: What is the main goal of just-in-time (JIT) inventory?
choices: Build large safety stocks to avoid any shortage
Increase warehouse space to hold more stock
Reduce holding costs by receiving goods close to when they are needed
questions.explain: JIT cuts holding costs by timing deliveries to need. Large safety stocks are the opposite approach.

questions.q: Orders wait 8 minutes at the kitchen pass in a restaurant. Which tool best sets priorities among the causes of slow service?
choices: Ratio analysis of the balance sheet
questions.explain: Pareto analysis ranks causes so the few that drive most delays get fixed first. The others evaluate money or profit, not causes.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of delegation?
choices: It removes all accountability from the manager
It frees managers for strategic work and develops employees' skills
It eliminates the need for training
questions.explain: Delegation spreads work and builds capability while the manager keeps overall accountability.

questions.q: A new employee arrives late repeatedly. What is the best first step under progressive discipline?
choices: Terminate the employee immediately without notice
Post the employee's attendance record publicly
Document the issue and hold a private coaching conversation
Ignore the issue until the annual review
questions.explain: Documentation and a private conversation are the fair first steps. Immediate termination skips the progressive process.

questions.q: A plant can produce 5,000 units per week and currently produces 4,000. What is its capacity utilization?
questions.explain: Capacity utilization is actual output divided by capacity, 4,000 divided by 5,000, which is 80 percent.

questions.q: A retailer collects sales tax from customers and sends it to the state. In this role, the retailer is acting as:
choices: A collection agent for the government
questions.explain: Sales tax is paid by the customer but collected and remitted by the seller on the government's behalf.

questions.q: Which tax is withheld from employee paychecks for Social Security and Medicare?
questions.explain: FICA funds Social Security and Medicare and is split between employer and employee. FUTA is an employer-only unemployment tax.

questions.q: A manager finds that a supplier is falsifying safety certificates. Which action is most ethical?
choices: Keep buying because the product is cheaper
Tell customers privately that the product is safe
Report the issue internally and stop purchasing until the supplier is verified
Ignore it since it is not the company's fault
questions.explain: Reporting and pausing purchases addresses the safety risk and is transparent. Ignoring it or misleading customers is unethical.

questions.q: Corporate social responsibility is best defined as:
choices: Paying only the legal minimum wage
Voluntary actions beyond legal requirements that benefit society
questions.explain: CSR is voluntary action beyond what the law requires, such as environmental or community programs.

questions.q: Which federal law prohibits contracts, combinations and conspiracies that unreasonably restrain trade?
questions.explain: The Sherman Act is the foundational antitrust statute on restraints of trade. The others address specific practices or agency powers.

questions.q: Which expense is generally fully deductible in the year it is paid by a small business?
choices: Monthly rent on the business's shop space
The purchase price of a new commercial building
questions.explain: Rent is an ordinary and necessary business expense, deductible when paid. Land is never depreciated, a commercial building is depreciated over 39 years, and a personal vacation is not a business expense.

questions.q: A business advertises that a product is 'clinically proven' without any supporting study. Which federal agency is most likely to act?
questions.explain: The FTC polices deceptive advertising. The SEC covers securities and the Fed covers monetary policy.

questions.q: Sole proprietors report business income and expenses on which IRS schedule attached to Form 1040?
questions.explain: Schedule C is the profit or loss from business form for sole proprietors. Form 1120 is a corporate return.

questions.q: Which federal law is the primary statute governing air pollution emissions?
questions.explain: The Clean Air Act regulates air emissions. The others cover water, species and waste.

questions.q: A business owner awards a contract to a company owned by a relative without disclosing it. This is a:
questions.explain: A conflict of interest exists when personal ties could compromise business decisions, and undisclosed ties make it worse.

questions.q: A partnership files Form 1065 but pays no federal income tax itself. Which form does it give each partner to report their share of income on their personal return?
questions.explain: A partnership is a pass-through entity: it files an information return (Form 1065) and gives each partner a Schedule K-1 showing their share. W-2s are for employees, 1099-NEC is for contractors, and Schedule C is for sole proprietors.

questions.q: A small business collects customers' emails for a newsletter. What is the best practice?
choices: Share the list with partners without notice
Buy extra lists from unknown sellers
Store all data in a public folder
Obtain consent and provide an easy opt-out
questions.explain: Consent and an easy opt-out are best practice, and the U.S. CAN-SPAM Act requires a working opt-out on commercial email. Sharing, buying or exposing lists breaks customer trust and privacy rules.

questions.q: A stakeholder is best defined as:
choices: Any person or group affected by the business's decisions
Only the business's owners and shareholders
questions.explain: Stakeholders include employees, customers, communities and others affected, not only owners.

questions.q: Which tax concept requires a business to pay tax during the year rather than only at filing?
questions.explain: Estimated tax payments are made quarterly by businesses and self-employed owners who do not have withholding.

questions.q: Which accounting principle requires reporting all information that could affect a user's decision?
questions.explain: Full disclosure requires material information to be reported. Historical cost, conservatism and matching are other principles.

questions.q: Which federal agency sets and enforces workplace safety standards?
questions.explain: OSHA sets and enforces workplace safety standards. The EPA covers environmental rules and the Wage and Hour Division covers pay.

vocab.def: A written document describing a business's goals, market, operations, and financial projections.
A short opening section of a business plan that summarizes the key findings and the funding request.
An analysis of whether a business idea is practical in terms of market, operations, finance and law.
A framework that lists a business's internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
The specific benefit a customer receives that makes an offer worth choosing over alternatives.
The specific group of customers with shared needs that a business chooses to serve.
Dividing a broad market into groups of customers with similar needs or characteristics.
A factor that lets a business outperform rivals and that rivals find hard to copy.
A calculation of the sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs, so profit is zero.
The simplest version of a product that lets a business test customer demand with minimal investment.
The four controllable elements of marketing (product, price, place and promotion), also called the 4 Ps.
The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
A pricing strategy that sets a high initial price and lowers it over time to reach successive market segments.
A pricing strategy that sets a low initial price to gain market share quickly.
The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
The added value a brand name gives a product, based on customer awareness, loyalty and perceived quality.
A word, name, symbol or design that identifies the source of goods and distinguishes them from others.
Unpaid media coverage about a business, which the business does not directly control.
Data collected directly by the business for its own purpose, such as surveys or focus groups.
The total gross profit a business expects from a customer over the full relationship.
Raising money by selling ownership shares or stakes in the business.
Raising money by borrowing that must be repaid with interest.
Current assets minus current liabilities, a measure of short-term liquidity.
Current assets divided by current liabilities, a measure of the ability to pay short-term obligations.
Gross profit divided by revenue, showing the share of each sales dollar left after cost of goods sold.
Revenue minus all expenses, including cost of goods sold, operating expenses, interest and taxes.
The systematic allocation of a long-term asset's cost over its useful life.
An accounting method that records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash timing.
Net profit divided by the cost of an investment, expressed as a percentage.
Payment terms from a supplier that allow a business to buy now and pay later, often with a discount for early payment.
A business owned and run by one person with no legal separation between owner and business.
A business owned by two or more people who share profits, losses and management.
A business entity that limits owners' personal liability for business debts and is taxed as a pass-through by default.
A corporation taxed separately from its owners, with dividends taxed again to shareholders.
A government grant giving an inventor exclusive rights to make, use and sell an invention for a set period.
Legal protection for original creative works, such as writing, music and software, held by the creator.
Confidential business information, such as a formula or process, that gives value because it is not public.
Something of value exchanged by each party to a contract, required for the contract to be enforceable.
A promise by an owner to repay a business debt personally if the business cannot pay.
A seller's or manufacturer's legal responsibility for injuries caused by a defective product.
The number of employees a manager directly supervises.
A system that receives materials only as they are needed for production, to cut holding costs.
